subject: ENGLISH LANGUAGE
title: Reading: Extensive Reading (Independent Reading)
overview: Extensive reading means reading widely on your own, for information and for enjoyment. In this sub-strand you will read sample newspaper and magazine texts about money, choose materials that suit your age and interests, and talk about what you read. The aim is a habit you can keep, including in a simple reading club.

lessons.title: Reading a newspaper and a magazine text
objectives: Read a short news-style article and a magazine-style article.
Pick out who, what and why.
Infer the meaning of money words from the text.
lessons.intro: A newspaper reports what happened. A magazine often explains or tells a short true story. Both can teach you about money if you read them for yourself, not only wait for a summary.
lessons.notes:
### How these texts are built
A news article often starts with the most important facts: who did something, what they did, and why it matters. A magazine piece may be more personal. It still needs a title. The samples below were written for this lesson. They are not reports from a real newspaper, and they do not use made-up figures.

### Sample news article
**Class Saves Coins for Tree Seedlings**

Learners in one Grade 4 class have started a saving tin. Each Friday, pupils who can spare a coin drop it in. Nobody is forced to pay. At the end of the month the class counts the coins together, writes the total in a book, and keeps the book in the teacher's cupboard.

The learners plan to buy tree seedlings for the school compound. Their teacher says the project teaches two habits: saving, and spending money on something the whole class chose. A monitor checks that the tin is closed. The class has agreed that the money will not be borrowed for snacks.

### Sample magazine article
**Market Morning**

I went to the market with my aunt. She sells vegetables. Before we left home she wrote a list: what she would buy, and the most she was willing to pay. At the market she compared prices. When a price was fair, she bought. When it was too high, she walked on.

A customer wanted credit, which means taking goods now and paying later. My aunt asked gently, 'Can you pay on Saturday?' They agreed, and she wrote the name and the amount in a notebook. She told me, 'A written record protects both of us.' We came home with fewer coins but with goods to sell. That is business: buying, selling, and keeping track.

### Words from the texts
Spare means you can give it without going without something you need. A total is the amount when everything is added. Credit, in this article, means taking goods now and paying later. A record is writing that helps you remember an agreement.

Read both texts again and be ready to retell them without looking.

keyWords.meaning: a piece of writing in a newspaper or magazine
an agreement to take goods or money now and pay later
a written note that keeps information
keeping money instead of spending it at once

examples.problem: Factual: What do the learners plan to buy with the coins?
steps: Look at the news article.
Find the sentence about their plan.
examples.answer: Tree seedlings for the school compound.

examples.problem: Inferential: Why did the aunt write the customer's name and the amount?
steps: She talks about a written record.
Both people need to remember the agreement.
examples.answer: So that both of them can remember the credit agreement.

activity.title: Read and retell
materials: A newspaper or magazine page if the class has one
steps: Read both samples silently.
In groups, retell one article each. The listeners may look back only to check a fact.
Underline credit, record and total, and say what each word means in the text.
If a real newspaper or magazine is available, find one headline about money or buying and read the first paragraph.

practice.question: Is every learner forced to put a coin in the tin?
practice.answer: No. Nobody is forced to pay.

practice.question: Where is the class record kept?
practice.answer: In a book in the teacher's cupboard.

practice.question: What does credit mean in Market Morning?
practice.answer: Taking goods now and paying later.

practice.question: Why did the aunt write a list before she left home?
practice.answer: To remember what to buy and the most she was willing to pay.

summary: News articles lead with the main facts. Magazine pieces may tell a personal true story.
These samples show saving, careful buying and a written record.
Retelling shows that you read for meaning.

lessons.title: Choosing what to read on your own
objectives: Choose a text that is suitable and interesting.
Show that you can read it without waiting to be told every step.
Share an opinion about what you read.
lessons.intro: Independent reading starts with a choice. A page you cannot yet read will only frustrate you. A page far below you will not teach you anything new. The right page is interesting and just challenging enough.
lessons.notes:
### How to choose
Look at the title, the pictures and the first few lines. Ask three questions.

- Is it interesting to me? Money, markets, sport, animals and school life are all fair interests. Choose one you actually want.
- Can I read most of the words? If you stop at every word, the text is too hard for independent reading. If you know every word at a glance, you can still enjoy it, but try a slightly richer page next time.
- Is it suitable? Choose material your teacher or family would be glad to see in your hands. Leave pages that are cruel, frightening or that ask for your personal details.

Newspapers and magazines are useful because the pieces are short. You can finish one article in a sitting. Digital copies count as reading too, if you stay on a page an adult has allowed.

### Show that you read
Independent reading is quiet, but it is not secret from learning. After you read:

- retell the piece in four or five sentences;
- write one new word and a meaning you inferred;
- say your opinion. Did the people in the text handle money wisely? Would you do the same?

An opinion needs a reason. 'I liked it' is a start. 'I liked it because the aunt wrote down the credit' is a reader's opinion.

### A reading time
You can read after homework, during a library lesson, or in a short slot the class agrees. Ten focused minutes are better than an hour of turning pages without looking. Keep a simple log: the date, the title and one sentence about what you learned.

keyWords.meaning: reading you choose and do yourself, for information or enjoyment
right for your age and safe to read
what you think about a text, backed by a reason
a short written list of what you have read

examples.problem: A page uses many words you cannot say, and there is no picture or heading you understand. Should you choose it for independent reading today?
steps: Independent reading should be mostly understandable.
You can ask a teacher to read a hard page with you another time.
examples.answer: No. Choose a clearer article today. You can return to the hard page with help.

examples.problem: Give an opinion, with a reason, about the aunt in Market Morning.
steps: Name what she did.
Say why that action was wise or unwise.
examples.answer: Example: I think she was wise because she wrote the name and the amount before she gave credit.

activity.title: Choose, read, speak
materials: Newspapers, magazines, storybooks or a school device with reading material
steps: Select one age-suitable text about money or another high-interest topic. Use the three questions: interesting, readable, suitable.
Read it alone for several quiet minutes.
Write the date, the title and one new word in your log.
In a group, retell the text and give an opinion with a reason.

practice.question: Name the three questions that help you choose a text.
practice.answer: Is it interesting? Can I read most of the words? Is it suitable?

practice.question: What can you write in a reading log?
practice.answer: The date, the title and one sentence or a new word from the text.

practice.question: Why is 'I liked it because the class counted the coins together' a better opinion than 'I liked it'?
practice.answer: It gives a reason from the text.

practice.question: What should you do with a page that asks for your personal details?
practice.answer: Leave it and tell an adult.

summary: Choose texts that are interesting, readable and suitable.
Retell, record and give an opinion with a reason.
A short regular reading time builds independence.

lessons.title: A habit and a reading club
objectives: Explain why independent reading should continue after school.
Set one reading goal you can actually keep.
lessons.intro: A single lesson can show you how to read widely. A habit keeps the skill alive. Clubs, libraries and a book beside your bed are all ways to carry reading into ordinary weeks.
lessons.notes:
### Why the habit matters
Independent reading makes you a lifelong learner. Newspapers and magazines change every week, so a reader who knows how to choose an article can keep learning about money, health, sport and the community without waiting for a new textbook.

Stories about money also show choices and consequences. A trader who gives credit without a record may forget the debt. A class that counts its tin together can see whether the plan is working. You do not copy every choice. You think about it.

### A simple club
An after-school reading club can meet once a week in a classroom or library. Members bring a book, a magazine or a printed article. For ten minutes everyone reads. Then each person tells one fact or one opinion. Roles can rotate: a timekeeper, a person who welcomes newcomers, and a person who looks after the books.

If the club also meets online, an adult should be present. Do not share your home details, photographs or passwords. The point of the meeting is the reading, not a chat with strangers.

### A goal you can keep
Choose a small goal and write it down. Examples: read one short article every week; finish one storybook this month; add four titles to a log. A goal that is too huge is easy to drop. Check the goal when the club meets, or ask a family member to look at your log.

Bring the money theme with you when you like. Read about markets, saving, fees and honest business. Also read other topics you love. Extensive reading grows when the choice stays yours.

The skill you are adopting is not 'finishing Grade 4 English'. It is picking up a suitable text, understanding it, and wanting to pick up another.

keyWords.meaning: continuing through your life, not only during one school term
a group that meets regularly for a shared activity
a result you decide to work towards
what happens because of a choice

examples.problem: Which goal is easier to keep: 'Read every book in the library' or 'Read one article a week and log it'?
steps: A goal should be clear and small enough to finish.
A log lets you check it.
examples.answer: Read one article a week and log it.

examples.problem: Name two rules for an online reading club.
steps: Think about safety and about the purpose of the club.
examples.answer: An adult should be present, and members should not share personal details or passwords. The meeting is for reading.

activity.title: Plan a reading club
steps: In groups, decide when a weekly club could meet and where.
List three club rules, including one about looking after books and one about kindness.
Each learner writes one personal reading goal for the next two weeks.
Share the goal with the group so that someone can ask you about it next time.

practice.question: Give one reason to keep reading newspapers or magazines after this lesson.
practice.answer: They are short, they change, and they help you learn about real topics such as money on your own.

practice.question: What happens in the ten quiet minutes of the club described here?
Why should an adult be present if a club meets online?
practice.answer: So that the meeting stays safe and is really about reading.

practice.question: Write one reading goal you could keep.
practice.answer: Example: I will read one short article each week and write the title in my log.

summary: Independent reading is a habit for learning and enjoyment beyond one lesson.
A club needs time to read, time to talk, and safe, kind rules.
A small written goal is easier to keep than a huge promise.

quiz.question: In the news sample, the coins are for
quiz.explanation: The class plans to buy tree seedlings.

quiz.question: Nobody is forced to put money in the tin. This means
options: giving a coin is a choice
the teacher keeps the coins secret from the class
credit is the same as a fine
quiz.explanation: The article says nobody is forced to pay.

quiz.question: In Market Morning, credit means
options: taking goods now and paying later
quiz.explanation: The article explains credit in that way.

quiz.question: Why did the aunt write the name and the amount?
options: so both people would remember the agreement
to avoid paying tax by lawless means
quiz.explanation: She says a written record protects both people.

quiz.question: Which text is the better choice for independent reading today?
options: A page where you know almost none of the words
A suitable article you find interesting and can mostly read
A page that asks for your photograph
quiz.explanation: The text should be interesting, readable and suitable.

quiz.question: A reading log should include
quiz.explanation: A simple log records the date and the title, plus a note if you wish.

quiz.question: A strong opinion
options: has a reason from the text
quiz.explanation: An opinion is stronger when you say why.

quiz.question: During the quiet part of the reading club, members
quiz.explanation: The plan gives ten minutes for everyone to read.

quiz.question: Why is independent reading useful for lifelong learning?
quiz.answer: You can keep choosing suitable texts, such as articles about money and other topics, and learn from them on your own.
quiz.explanation: The habit continues after a single lesson or textbook.

quiz.question: What is one safe rule for an online reading club?
quiz.answer: An adult should be present, and members should not share personal details or passwords.
quiz.explanation: The club is for reading, and personal information stays private.
